requirements: Reproduce the MEP-based LLM framework for GPU kernel optimization and its reported speedups on PolyBench (NVIDIA & DCU), AMD APP SDK, and three large-scale HPC application hotspot kernels.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware and software environments (NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti with CUDA 11.5/Ubuntu 22.04, Haiguang DCU with HIP 24.04/CentOS 7) and the OpenAI o3 LLM API access are configured as described in Section 4.1.
The NVIDIA GPU platform (Platform 1) is provisioned with the exact hardware/software stack specified in Section 4.1.
Code has been implemented that verifies an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU is present and accessible on Platform 1 (e.g., via `nvidia-smi` or a CUDA device query utility).
Code has been implemented that installs and validates CUDA Toolkit 11.5 (nvcc --version reports 11.5) on Platform 1.
Code has been implemented that verifies Platform 1 runs Ubuntu 22.04 (e.g., via `lsb_release -a` or `/etc/os-release` inspection).
Code has been implemented that compiles and runs a minimal CUDA test kernel on the RTX 2080 Ti to confirm the CUDA 11.5 toolchain is functional end-to-end.
The Haiguang DCU platform (Platform 2) is provisioned with the AMD-licensed accelerator and HIP toolchain specified in Section 4.1.

Code has been implemented that verifies a Haiguang DCU accelerator (AMD-licensed architecture) is present and accessible on Platform 2 (e.g., via `rocm-smi`/`hy-smi` or an equivalent DCU device query).
Code has been implemented that installs and validates the HIP 24.04 programming stack (hipcc/`hipconfig` reports version 24.04) on Platform 2.
Code has been implemented that verifies Platform 2 runs CentOS 7 (e.g., via `/etc/centos-release` or `/etc/os-release`).
Code has been implemented that compiles and runs a minimal HIP test kernel on the DCU to confirm the HIP 24.04 toolchain is functional end-to-end.
OpenAI o3 API access is configured and integrated into the framework's LLM-invocation pathway.
Code has been implemented that configures an OpenAI API client using the `o3` model identifier and reads the API key from a secure source (e.g., environment variable).
Code has been implemented that performs a live sanity-check request to the OpenAI o3 API on startup, confirming authenticated access before optimization begins.
Code has been implemented that provides a unified LLM invocation wrapper used by MEP construction, AER, and iterative optimization, so all LLM calls route through the o3-configured client.

Code has been implemented that selects the correct platform-specific toolchain (CUDA 11.5 on Platform 1, HIP 24.04 on Platform 2) at build time so the same framework can drive PolyBench on NVIDIA and PolyBench/AMD APP SDK/HPC applications on DCU.

The PolyBench GPU suite (20 kernels), AMD APP SDK (12 sample programs), and the three large-scale HPC applications (LAMMPS, MISA-MD, xblue) with their hotspot kernels are obtained and prepared for use as evaluation targets across NVIDIA and DCU platforms.
The PolyBench GPU benchmark suite is acquired and prepared with both CUDA (NVIDIA) and HIP (DCU) variants.
Code has been implemented to fetch/clone the PolyBench GPU suite from https://github.com/sgrauerg/polybenchGpu and place it under a known directory used by the framework.
Code has been implemented to select and register the 20 PolyBench GPU kernels covering matrix, sparse, and correlation computations as the PolyBench evaluation set.

The PolyBench kernel set explicitly includes at least the kernels reported in Tables 1 and 2 (2MM, 3MM, ADI, ATAX, BICG, CORR, COVAR, GEMM, GEMVER, GESUMMV, GRAMSCHM, SYR2K, SYRK) with sources locatable per kernel.
Code has been implemented to build the original CUDA PolyBench kernels on the NVIDIA platform to obtain baseline reference binaries.
Code has been implemented to port the PolyBench CUDA kernels to HIP (via hipify or equivalent) so the same 20 kernels can be built and run on the Haiguang DCU platform.

Code has been implemented to extract, for each PolyBench kernel, the isolated GPU kernel source (signature, body, and required data structures) so it can be handed to the MEP construction stage independently of the full benchmark build.
The 12 AMD APP SDK sample programs are acquired and prepared for DCU-only evaluation.
Code or documented setup steps have been implemented to obtain the AMD APP SDK sample sources (referenced from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMD_APP_SDK) and place them under a known directory.

Code has been implemented to select and register 12 representative AMD APP SDK sample programs covering image processing, signal transformation, and basic vector/matrix operations, including at least binomialoption, bitonicsort, dwthaar1d, fastwalshtransform, matrixmultiplication, reduction, simpleconvolution, and vectoradd (from Table 3).
Code has been implemented to build each of the 12 AMD APP SDK samples under HIP on the DCU platform, yielding runnable baseline binaries.
Code has been implemented to extract the hotspot GPU kernel from each AMD APP SDK sample so it can be provided to MEP construction independently of the sample's full build.
The three large-scale HPC applications (LAMMPS, MISA-MD, xblue) and their specific hotspot kernels are acquired and prepared for DCU evaluation.
Code or documented steps have been implemented to obtain the LAMMPS source (from https://www.lammps.org/) and build it on the DCU platform with HIP support.
Code has been implemented to extract the LAMMPS hotspot kernel k_energy_fast (source, signature, and required inputs) from the LAMMPS codebase for use as an independent optimization target.
Code or documented steps have been implemented to obtain the MISA-MD source (from https://misa-md.github.io/MDoc/) and build it on the DCU platform.
Code has been implemented to extract the MISA-MD hotspot kernel md_nei_itl_wf_atom_soa as an independent optimization target.
Documented steps or acquisition scripts have been provided to obtain the xblue CFD application source and build it on the DCU platform (Oriental Supercomputer environment).
Code has been implemented to extract the xblue hotspot kernel gauss_all_seidel_backfor as an independent optimization target.
Code has been implemented to run each HPC application end-to-end with the original hotspot kernel to establish a baseline integrated runtime used later for Integrated Speedup measurements.
A unified dataset/registry glues the three sources together and enforces platform assignment consistent with Section 4.1.

Code has been implemented to maintain a benchmark registry that tags each kernel with its suite (PolyBench / AMD APP SDK / HPC), target platforms (NVIDIA and/or DCU), and iterative-optimization parameters (D=6,N=3 for PolyBench; D=10,N=5 for AMD APP SDK and HPC applications).
Code has been implemented that ensures AMD APP SDK and the three HPC applications are only dispatched to the DCU platform, while PolyBench is dispatched to both NVIDIA and DCU platforms.
Implement the automatic MEP construction that completes an independently extracted hotspot kernel into a runnable program satisfying the T_ker >= T_min and T_overall <= T_max constraints.

Hotspot kernel intake and parsing: the framework accepts an independently extracted GPU kernel and extracts the information (signature, parameters, launch shape, dependencies) needed to build a MEP around it.
Code has been implemented that accepts an independently extracted hotspot kernel source (CUDA or HIP) as input to MEP construction without requiring the full application source tree.
Code has been implemented that parses the kernel's signature, including argument names, types (including pointer/array parameters), and qualifiers (e.g., __global__/__device__, __restrict__).

Code has been implemented that analyzes the kernel body to identify its computational logic (loop structure, memory-access patterns, shared-memory usage) so the completion can preserve functional logic.

Code has been implemented that detects external symbols/types the kernel depends on (structs, typedefs, macros, helper device functions) and records them so the MEP can include stub/replacement definitions.

LLM-driven completion into a runnable program: given the parsed kernel, an LLM assembles a self-contained MEP that handles input preparation, memory allocation, kernel invocation, and result handling.
Code has been implemented that invokes the OpenAI o3 LLM via API with a prompt containing the extracted kernel and instructions to generate a complete MEP source file.

The generated MEP contains host-side setup code performing device memory allocation (cudaMalloc/hipMalloc), host-to-device transfers, and post-run device-to-host retrieval for the kernel's inputs and outputs.
The generated MEP contains a kernel invocation with a grid/block configuration consistent with the original kernel's launch parameters and problem size.
The generated MEP contains result-handling code that copies outputs back and either checksums or dumps them to a canonical form for later Functional Equivalence checks.
The generated MEP is a self-contained source that compiles independently of the original application (only standard toolchain headers/libraries such as CUDA/HIP runtime, no project-internal headers).
Code has been implemented that emits the same MEP structure for both CUDA (NVIDIA) and HIP (DCU) backends, selecting API names/headers based on the target platform.
Instrumentation for timing T_ker and T_overall: the MEP measures the average per-invocation kernel execution time and the total program execution time used to check the time constraints.
Code has been implemented that instruments the kernel launch with GPU event timing (cudaEvent/hipEvent) and computes T_ker as the average kernel execution time over the launches in one MEP run.
Code has been implemented that measures T_overall as the total end-to-end MEP execution time (including data generation/transfer/kernel/result-handling) for use in the T_overall <= T_max check.
The MEP reports T_ker and T_overall on a machine-readable output channel (stdout or file) that the framework can parse for constraint checking.

Problem-size selection enforcing the constraints T_ker >= T_min and T_overall <= T_max (Equation 1): the MEP builder chooses a workload size that makes kernel execution measurable while keeping the total run within budget.
Code has been implemented that exposes configurable T_min and T_max thresholds for the MEP-time constraints of Equation (1).
Code has been implemented that automatically selects an initial problem size for the MEP by parsing kernel parameters and launch logic, either LLM-suggested or heuristically derived.
Code has been implemented that runs the MEP with the candidate problem size, reads back T_ker and T_overall, and evaluates whether both T_ker >= T_min and T_overall <= T_max are satisfied.
When T_ker < T_min, the framework increases the workload (larger problem size or additional repetition of the kernel launch) and re-measures until the threshold is met or an upper cap is reached.
When T_overall > T_max, the framework decreases the workload (smaller problem size or fewer launches) and re-measures until the total time drops within budget.
Code has been implemented that terminates MEP construction with an explicit error/status when no problem size can simultaneously satisfy T_ker >= T_min and T_overall <= T_max.

Baseline evaluation and hand-off to downstream stages: once a valid MEP is constructed, the framework records the baseline kernel version K^(0) and its measured baseline performance to feed the Iterative Optimization stage (per Figure 2).
Code has been implemented that compiles and executes the constructed MEP end-to-end on the target platform to record a baseline T_ker used as K^(0)'s performance reference.

Code has been implemented that triggers Automatic Error Repair (feeding erroneous code, diagnostics, and abnormal outputs back to the LLM) whenever MEP construction produces compilation errors, runtime errors, or inconsistent outputs.
Code has been implemented that hands off the finalized MEP (source, chosen problem size, baseline timing) to the Performance-Feedback Iterative Optimization stage as the initial baseline K^(0).
Implement the Input Data Generator that produces kernel inputs matching the extracted kernel's pattern under the S_data <= S_max constraint for repeatable MEP evaluation.
The Input Data Generator infrastructure exists and is invoked as part of MEP construction after kernel completion.

Code has been implemented that defines an Input Data Generator module/component that is invoked after MEP code completion and before performance evaluation, producing the runtime inputs consumed by the MEP.

Code has been implemented that parses the extracted hotspot kernel's signature (argument names, types, shapes, and pointer/array parameters) so the generator knows what buffers and scalars must be produced.

Code has been implemented that drives the generator via the LLM (or a template guided by the LLM's analysis of kernel logic) so the produced inputs match the extracted kernel's input pattern (dtypes, ranges, sparsity, layout).
The generator enforces the S_data <= S_max data-size constraint from Equation (2) so total MEP execution stays within T_max.
Code has been implemented that measures and reports S_data (the total generated input size in bytes/MB) for every generated input set.
Code has been implemented that exposes a configurable S_max upper bound and rejects/regenerates any input whose measured S_data exceeds S_max, enforcing the constraint from Equation (2).

Code has been implemented that couples the generator's problem-size selection to the T_overall <= T_max budget, adjusting input dimensions when the resulting MEP runtime would violate the time budget defined in Section 3.1.1.
The generator produces repeatable, deterministic inputs that make kernel timing stable across runs and candidates.

Code has been implemented that uses a fixed/seeded random number generator (or otherwise deterministic construction) so the same kernel is fed identical inputs across the baseline, all candidates within a round, and across rounds.
Code has been implemented that persists or reproducibly regenerates the input set so R=30 repeated timing runs and Functional Equivalence checks operate on identical inputs.
Code has been implemented that allocates and initializes both host and device buffers of the requested sizes and copies the generated inputs to the GPU/DCU device memory prior to kernel invocation.
The generator supports the full set of kernel input shapes encountered across PolyBench, AMD APP SDK, and the HPC hotspot kernels.
Code has been implemented that generates dense matrix / vector inputs (row/column-major, float/double) as required by PolyBench-style kernels (e.g., 2MM, GEMM, GEMVER, CORR, COVAR).

Code has been implemented that generates specialized input patterns needed by non-GEMM kernels in AMD APP SDK and HPC applications (e.g., power-of-two lengths for bitonicsort/FFT-like kernels, neighbor lists / atom arrays for LAMMPS and MISA-MD, stencil grids for xblue).

Implement Automatic Error Repair (AER) that feeds errors/diagnostics/abnormal outputs back to the LLM, and Functional Equivalence (FE) validation via output consistency checks used during both completion and iterative optimization.
Automatic Error Repair (AER) subsystem detects faults and drives LLM-based repair using diagnostics feedback.
Fault detection: compilation, runtime, and output-inconsistency error capture.

Code has been implemented to invoke the platform compiler (nvcc for CUDA / hipcc for HIP) on generated candidates and capture stdout, stderr, and non-zero exit codes as a structured compilation-error diagnostic record.

Code has been implemented to execute the compiled MEP under a timeout wrapper and capture runtime failures (non-zero exit codes, CUDA/HIP API error strings, segmentation faults, and timeouts) as a structured runtime-error diagnostic record.

Code has been implemented that flags a candidate as producing 'abnormal outputs' when its kernel output diverges from the baseline output during Functional Equivalence checks, packaging the divergence details (indices, expected vs actual values) into a diagnostic record.
Repair prompt construction and LLM feedback loop.

Code has been implemented that builds an AER repair prompt containing (i) the erroneous kernel/MEP source code, (ii) the captured compiler/runtime diagnostics, and (iii) any abnormal-output samples, and submits it to the configured LLM (OpenAI o3) via API.

Code has been implemented so that AER is invoked automatically both during MEP construction/completion (Section 3.1) and during each iterative optimization round (Section 3.2), sharing the same repair mechanism across stages.

Code has been implemented with a bounded AER retry loop that re-attempts repair up to a configured maximum number of iterations, exiting successfully when the repaired candidate compiles, runs, and passes FE, and marking the candidate as failed otherwise.
Code has been implemented that parses the LLM's repair response, extracts a full replacement kernel/MEP source, and re-enters the compile -> run -> FE-check pipeline with the new candidate.
AER behavioral tests confirm that each fault class triggers repair and that repaired candidates are re-validated.
On a deliberately broken kernel that fails to compile, AER is triggered, the compiler diagnostics appear in the prompt sent to the LLM, and the loop advances only after a successful recompilation.
On a kernel that compiles but crashes at runtime (e.g., illegal memory access), AER is triggered and the runtime error string is forwarded to the LLM in the repair prompt.
Functional Equivalence (FE) validation via output consistency checks used during completion and iterative optimization.
Baseline output capture and comparison infrastructure.
Code has been implemented that runs the baseline kernel K^(d) on the Input-Data-Generator-produced input and stores its device output buffer(s) as the reference for FE comparison in round d.
Code has been implemented that executes each candidate K^(d,n) on the identical input tensors used for the baseline, so that FE comparisons are made against byte-identical inputs.

Code has been implemented that compares candidate outputs against the baseline reference element-wise using a numerical tolerance (absolute and/or relative) appropriate to the floating-point precision of the kernel, and returns a boolean pass/fail plus per-element divergence statistics.
Integration of FE into candidate feasible-set selection.
Code has been implemented that builds the feasible set F^(d) = { n : candidate K^(d,n) satisfies FE against K^(d) }, and restricts the next-baseline argmin selection (Section 3.2) to n in F^(d).

Code has been implemented that excludes any candidate failing FE from Speedup statistics, in accordance with the paper's rule that 'only optimizations passing Functional Equivalence verification are included in Speedup statistics'.
Code has been implemented that, on an FE violation, routes the failing candidate together with the divergence report into the AER repair loop rather than silently discarding it.
FE behavioral tests confirm correct pass/fail decisions and correct exclusion behavior.
Given a semantically-equivalent candidate (e.g., a re-tiled kernel producing the same output within tolerance), the FE check returns pass and the candidate enters the feasible set F^(d).

Given a candidate that deliberately alters kernel semantics (e.g., wrong reduction order producing outputs outside tolerance), the FE check returns fail, the candidate is excluded from F^(d), and AER is invoked.

Implement the multi-round iterative optimization loop that generates N candidates per round guided by profiler feedback, evaluates with R runs and trimmed mean, enforces functional equivalence, selects the next baseline, and applies Performance Pattern Inheritance.
The optimization loop drives D rounds of candidate generation and selection, starting from an initial baseline K^(0) and updating K^(d) after each round.

Code has been implemented for a top-level iterative optimization driver function that accepts a baseline MEP/kernel K^(0), number of rounds D, candidates per round N, and returns the best optimized kernel found.
Code has been implemented so the loop maintains a current baseline K^(d) across rounds and updates it to the round's selected best candidate at the start of round d+1.

Code has been implemented for a configurable termination condition that halts iteration when d == D OR when the round-over-round improvement in trimmed-mean kernel time falls below a preset threshold.
The driver exposes D and N as parameters and supports the paper's configurations: (D=6, N=3) for PolyBench and (D=10, N=5) for AMD APP SDK and large-scale HPC applications.
Each round generates up to N candidate kernels via the LLM, guided by profiler-derived performance feedback.
Code has been implemented that collects profiler feedback (e.g., cache hit rate, occupancy, and other GPU profiling counters) on the current baseline K^(d) before candidate generation each round.
Code has been implemented that constructs the LLM prompt for candidate generation by including the current baseline kernel source, the collected profiler metrics, and optimization guidance.
Code has been implemented that requests up to N candidate kernels {K^(d,n)} per round from the LLM (OpenAI o3) via API, storing each candidate for downstream evaluation.

The candidate generation call is wrapped in the Automatic Error Repair path so that compilation or runtime failures during candidate build/evaluation are fed back to the LLM to trigger repair attempts within the round.
Each candidate is measured with R repeated runs and its performance summarized by a trimmed mean that drops the k lowest and k highest samples, per Equation (3).
Code has been implemented that, for each candidate K^(d,n), runs the MEP R times and records the per-run average kernel execution time T_ker^(d,n) for each run.
Code has been implemented that sorts the R measurements ascendingly and discards the lowest k and highest k samples before averaging the remaining R-2k values, matching Equation (3).
The trimmed-mean routine uses R=30 runs and k=3 (dropping the top 3 and bottom 3) as reported in the experimental setup.
Given a synthetic ascending sequence of R=30 timing values, the trimmed_mean(k=3) function returns the arithmetic mean of the middle 24 values (indices 3..26 inclusive).
Functional Equivalence is enforced on all candidates and only FE-passing candidates are considered when selecting the next baseline, per Equations (4)-(5).
Code has been implemented that validates each candidate K^(d,n) against the baseline K^(d) via output consistency checks (Functional Equivalence) before including it in performance ranking.

Code has been implemented that constructs the feasible candidate set F^(d) = { K^(d,n) : FE(K^(d,n), K^(d)) holds } as defined in Equation (4), excluding any candidate that fails FE, compilation, or runtime execution.
When all N candidates in a round fail FE or execution, the loop retains the previous baseline K^(d) as K^(d+1) and continues (or terminates) rather than crashing.
The next-round baseline is selected as the FE-passing candidate with the minimum trimmed-mean kernel execution time, per Equation (5).
Code has been implemented that computes K^(d+1) = argmin over K^(d,n) in F^(d) of the trimmed-mean kernel time T_ker^(d,n), matching Equation (5).
The selection routine additionally guards against regressions: if the best feasible candidate's trimmed mean is not better than the current baseline's, the baseline is kept for the next round.
Given a synthetic round with N=3 candidates whose trimmed-mean times are [1.2, 0.8, 1.0] and all pass FE, the selection routine returns the candidate with time 0.8 as K^(d+1).
Performance Pattern Inheritance summarizes effective optimization patterns from successful rounds and injects them as constraints/hints into subsequent rounds' prompts.

Code has been implemented that, after each round, extracts a summary of the winning candidate's optimization patterns (e.g., tiling choices, memory coalescing, synchronization restructuring) via an LLM-driven analysis step.
Code has been implemented that maintains a running pattern memory across rounds and injects it as constraints or hints into the LLM prompt for candidate generation in subsequent rounds.

The inherited patterns are also passed across platforms/kernels when applicable so that strategies discovered on one MEP can seed prompts for related kernels, supporting cross-platform reuse as claimed.
The loop logs per-round diagnostics needed to reproduce speedup tables and analyses.
Code has been implemented that logs, for each round d and each candidate n, the R raw timings, the trimmed mean, the FE pass/fail status, and any AER events, to a structured file (e.g., JSON or CSV).
Code has been implemented that records the selected baseline K^(d+1) source and its trimmed-mean time per round, enabling reconstruction of the optimization trajectory and final Standalone Speedup.

depends_on: Automatic Error Repair and Functional Equivalence

sub_tasks.requirements: Implement the three reported metrics (Standalone Speedup in MEP, Integrated Speedup after reintegration, and Direct LLM Optimization Speedup baseline) with R=30, k=3 trimmed-mean averaging, and FE-gated inclusion.
Implement the trimmed-mean timing procedure that repeats each candidate kernel execution and aggregates measurements according to Equation (3).
Code has been implemented that measures the average kernel execution time T_ker for a given candidate by running it R times and returning per-run timings, with R exposed as a configurable parameter.
Code has been implemented that sorts the R measured runtimes ascendingly and discards the lowest k and highest k values before averaging the remaining R-2k samples, matching Equation (3).
The trimmed-mean routine uses R=30 repetitions and k=3 discarded values on each side by default, matching the paper's reported settings.

Given a synthetic input array of 30 timings with known outliers at both extremes, the trimmed-mean function returns the arithmetic mean of the middle 24 values (indices 3 through 26 after sorting) within floating-point tolerance.
Implement the three speedup metrics reported in Section 4.1 using the trimmed-mean baseline and candidate timings.
Code has been implemented that computes Speedup = t_baseline / t_optimized (Equation 6) using trimmed-mean average execution times.
Code has been implemented that computes Standalone Speedup by measuring both the baseline kernel and the optimized kernel entirely within the MEP environment and taking their trimmed-mean time ratio.

Code has been implemented that computes Integrated Speedup by reintegrating the optimized kernel into the original full application, running the application to obtain the kernel's runtime in-context, and dividing the original application's kernel time by the reintegrated kernel time.

Code has been implemented that computes Direct LLM Optimization Speedup as the ratio of baseline time to the time of a single LLM-generated kernel obtained without any performance-feedback iterative loop (D=1, no profiler feedback, no pattern inheritance).
Enforce Functional Equivalence gating so that only FE-passing candidates contribute to reported speedup statistics.

Code has been implemented that, before including any candidate in speedup aggregation, verifies its output matches the baseline via the FE validation routine and excludes candidates that fail (or records them as errors, e.g., the 'Err' entry for dwthaar1d in Table 3).

When aggregating averages across a benchmark suite, the reporting code excludes FE-failing entries from the mean speedup computation while still listing them in the per-kernel table with an error marker.
Provide a unified measurement driver that produces all three metrics per kernel in a consistent, reproducible form.

Code has been implemented that, for each benchmark kernel, produces a record with fields {Standalone, Integrated, Direct LLM Optimization} using the same trimmed-mean settings (R=30, k=3), matching the columns of Tables 1-4.
The measurement driver reports speedup values rounded to two decimal places and computes the arithmetic mean across included kernels as the 'Average' row shown in Tables 1-4.
Reproduce the PolyBench per-kernel and average speedups on the NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti platform (D=6, N=3) reported in Table 1, including standalone 5.29x, integrated 5.05x, and direct LLM 2.10x averages.
Experimental configuration and infrastructure needed to run the PolyBench sweep on NVIDIA with D=6, N=3, R=30, k=3.

Code has been implemented that drives the framework over the 13 PolyBench kernels listed in Table 1 (2MM, 3MM, ADI, ATAX, BICG, CORR, COVAR, GEMM, GEMVER, GESUMMV, GRAMSCHM, SYR2K, SYRK) on the NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti platform.
Code has been implemented that sets the PolyBench iterative optimization parameters to D=6 rounds and N=3 candidates per round as specified in Section 4.1.
Code has been implemented that measures each candidate with R=30 repeated runs and computes a trimmed mean discarding the top-3 and bottom-3 (k=3) measurements before averaging.
Code has been implemented that invokes OpenAI o3 via API with the framework's performance-feedback prompt for the PolyBench NVIDIA runs.
Code has been implemented that compiles kernels with CUDA 11.5 targeting the NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti (compute capability 7.5) under Ubuntu 22.04.

Code has been implemented that, for each of the 13 kernels, reports Standalone Speedup (in MEP), Integrated Speedup (after reintegration into the PolyBench harness), and Direct LLM Optimization Speedup (no feedback loop) as separate columns.
Code has been implemented that filters out kernels whose optimized versions fail Functional Equivalence verification before including them in speedup statistics.

The regression-detection check reports zero flagged kernels across the Large-Scale HPC suite (LAMMPS, MISA-MD, xblue), consistent with the Section 4.4 claim that no cases showed expected gains in standalone tests but regressions upon integration.
Measured claims that Standalone averages closely track Integrated averages across suites.

The computed PolyBench NVIDIA average Standalone speedup (paper: 5.29x) is close to the average Integrated speedup (paper: 5.05x), with the absolute difference between the two averages within a small tolerance as reported in Table 1.
The computed PolyBench DCU average Standalone speedup (paper: 7.81x) is close to the average Integrated speedup (paper: 7.77x), reproducing the close alignment reported in Table 2.

The computed Large-Scale HPC average Standalone speedup (paper: 1.78x) versus average Integrated speedup (paper: 1.25x) reproduces the direction and magnitude of the gap reported in Table 4, demonstrating that standalone predictions remain in the same regime as integrated results while showing the acknowledged environment-fidelity gap.
